entries.topicDescription: Adding new functionality to existing classes without inheritance.

tips.title: Add methods to any class
tips.content:
Extension functions let you add new functions to existing classes 
without modifying their source code or using inheritance.

The class you extend is called the "receiver". Inside the function, 
you access the receiver's members with 'this' (which can be omitted).

Extensions are resolved statically at compile time — 
they don't actually modify the class. They're syntactic sugar for 
a static utility function with the receiver as the first parameter.

tips.title: Extension properties
tips.content:
You can also define extension properties, not just functions.
Since extensions can't store state, they can only have 
custom getters (and setters for var with a backing mechanism).

Extension properties are great for computed values 
that feel natural as properties rather than function calls.
tips.codeSnippet:
val String.wordCount: Int
    get() = this.trim().split("\\s+".toRegex()).size

// Usage
"Hello World".wordCount  // 2
"Kotlin is great".wordCount  // 3

tips.title: Extensions on nullable types
tips.content:
You can define extensions on nullable types (T?). 
This lets you call the function even on null references 
without a null check at the call site.

Inside the extension, 'this' can be null, so you must handle it.

Kotlin's stdlib uses this pattern — that's why you can call 
toString() on a nullable variable without ?. operator.
tips.codeSnippet:
fun String?.orEmpty(): String = this ?: ""

fun String?.isNullOrBlank(): Boolean =
    this == null || this.isBlank()

// Usage — no ?. needed!
val name: String? = null
name.orEmpty()       // ""
name.isNullOrBlank() // true

tips.title: A member function always wins over an extension
tips.content:
If a class has a member function and you declare an extension with the same name and parameters, calls resolve to the member; the extension is never called, and the compiler warns that it is shadowed. Extensions cannot override or replace members.

An extension with a different signature is fine — it just acts as an overload. This is why an extension can't change how an existing class behaves; it can only add to it.
tips.codeSnippet:
class Greeter { fun greet() = "member" }

fun Greeter.greet() = "extension"          // warning: shadowed by the member

fun Greeter.greet(name: String) = "hi $name" // different signature: a real overload

println(Greeter().greet())        // member
println(Greeter().greet("Ana"))   // hi Ana

tips.title: Member extensions have two receivers
tips.content:
An extension can be declared inside a class. Then it has two receivers: the extension receiver (the type being extended) and the dispatch receiver (an instance of the enclosing class). It is only usable where the dispatch receiver is available, which makes it a way to scope a helper to one class or builder.

When both receivers have a member with the same name, the extension receiver wins, and you reach the dispatch receiver with a label such as this@HtmlBuilder.

tips.title: Extend a companion object to add factory functions
tips.content:
An extension can target a class's companion object, so you can add what looks like a static factory to a type. The class must declare a companion object, even an empty one, for this to work.

That is useful for adding conversions and constructors from another module without editing the class. Keep in mind it only works for classes that have a companion, so you can't do it for most Java classes.
tips.codeSnippet:
class Money(val cents: Long) {
    companion object              // must exist, even if empty
}

fun Money.Companion.zero() = Money(0)
fun Money.Companion.fromDollars(d: Double) = Money((d * 100).toLong())

val price = Money.fromDollars(9.99)
val none = Money.zero()

tips.title: Constrain generic extensions with a bound
tips.content:
An extension can be generic, and a type bound restricts which receivers it accepts and unlocks operations on them. A bound of Comparable<T> lets the extension compare elements; a reified type parameter lets an inline extension use the type at runtime.

The bound keeps the extension out of code where it wouldn't make sense: calling isSorted on a list of objects that can't be compared is a compile error, not a runtime crash.

tips.title: An extension is only visible where it is declared or imported
tips.content:
A top-level extension belongs to the package where it is declared, and you must import it to use it from a different package, just like any function. That is why the same extension can be present in one file and unresolved in another. A private extension is visible only in its own file, and a member extension only inside its class.

Put related extensions in a clearly named file (StringExt.kt) and make them private if they are just helpers for one file.

tips.title: Know when not to write an extension
tips.content:
Extensions are convenient, but they have costs. An extension on a very general type (Any, T, String) shows up in autocomplete everywhere and can clash with a member added by a later library version. One that hides a side effect (network, disk) looks like a cheap property access.

Write a plain function when there is no natural receiver, keep extensions on general types private or narrowly scoped, and don't use one to hide business logic that belongs in a named class.
